title_content.content: Study of 5‑Alkynylpyrimidines as Cobalt Superfilling Inhibitors

paragraph_content.content: Haidi Li, Tao Zhang, Shiqi Song, Qian Li, Rongze Han, Qiaoxia Li, Yulin Min, Lina Qiu, Xixun Shen,* and Qunjie Xu*
Cite This: J. Phys. Chem. C 2025, 129, 232−243
Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More

ABSTRACT: Electrodeposition technology is the key core technology for achieving micro/nanoscale interconnection in high-end chip manufacturing. Recently, cobalt interconnect structures have been the ideal choice for constructing electronic pathways in process nodes below 14 nm due to the fact that cobalt has a smaller electron mean free path compared to copper; thus, studying the electroplating filling behavior of cobalt in micronano scale space has become a hot topic in the field of chip manufacturing. In this article, an electroplating solution containing a new 5-alkynylpyrimidine (5-EP) as an inhibitor is designed for electrochemical tests, including cyclic voltammetry and linear sweep voltammetry. The results indicate that the 5-EP significantly inhibits cobalt electrodeposition. The change in the nucleation mode of cobalt in an electroplating solution with the inhibitor (5-EP) was revealed by chronoamperometry, where cobalt atoms nucleate in a three-dimensional continuous manner instead of three-dimensional instantaneous nucleation. In situ enhanced Raman spectroscopy is used to further analyze the adsorption of the inhibitor (5-EP) molecules on the cobalt surface during the electroplating process from a spectroscopic perspective. The energy gap value of the additive molecule obtained through quantum chemical calculations is
\begin{array} { r } { \triangle E = E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } } - \bar { E _ { \mathrm { H O M O } } } = 3 . 3 0 2 ~ \mathrm { e V } , } \end{array}

indicating that the additive molecule has high reactivity and higher adsorption strength at the metal interface. The calculated electrostatic potential (ESP) values of the molecule range from a minimum of −47.29 kJ/mol to a maximum of 70.89 kJ/mol. Lower ESP values imply higher electron density. Molecular dynamics simulations calculate the adsorption energy of the additive molecule (5-EP) on Co(100) to be −133.96 kcal/mol, indicating that the 5-EP molecule has good adsorption capability. Electroplating experiments reveal that the addition of 6 ppm 5-EP to the plating solution enables defect-free filling of blind holes. Finally, it is also revealed by characterization tests (scanning electron microscopy/atomic force microscopy/X-ray difraction) that the inhibitor (5-EP) efectively reduces the surface roughness of the cobalt coating and, meantime, promotes the preferential growth of cobalt along the 100 and 110 crystal planes.

Damascene copper plating technology has remained the best choice for metal interconnects in logic chips and memory chips.<sup>1</sup> As semiconductor processes advance toward 10 nm and below, the use of copper as a conductor material begins to encounter issues with RC delay, which severely impacts the interconnect performance of chips. This has led to bottlenecks in process technology at the 10- and 7-nanometer nodes,<sup>2,3</sup> necessitating the search for new alternative interconnect materials. Researchers have found that metals such as Co, Ni, Mo, and Nb show greater potential than Cu.<sup>4</sup> However, when considering other parameters such as process and material costs, only Co is highlighted as a promising material. It has been reported that Co has already been used in the contact interconnect layers at the 10 nm node and is also considered suitable for use as a conductor in higher metal layers.<sup>5</sup> Compared to copper, cobalt has a shorter mean free path for electrons and a higher melting point. At the nanoscale, cobalt interconnects exhibit minimal size efects and superior resistance to electromigration.<sup>6</sup> The deposition quality of chip interconnect materials has a crucial impact on the final performance of the chip, directly afecting the chip’s yield, reliability, and stability. This places higher demands on the chip interconnect process. Electroplating technology is the primary technique for forming micro and nano interconnect structures.<sup>7</sup> In this complex process, additives play a critical role in regulating the deposition quality and behavior of metals.<sup>8</sup> Similar to the traditional Damascene copper interconnect process, the cobalt interconnect plating system also requires additives that can increase the metal deposition overpotential to achieve void-free superfilling in micro and nano structures.<sup>9</sup> The cobalt superfilling additives reported to date often contain unsaturated carbon bonds, nitrogencontaining functional groups, or a combination of both. The nitrogen-containing functional groups exist in the forms of amines
( - \mathrm { N H } _ { 2 } , \mathsf { \Gamma } - \mathrm { N H } )
, oxime groups
( - \mathrm { C = N - O H } )

and nitrogen-containing heterocycles. Utilizing the S-shaped negative diferential resistance (S-NDR) mechanism for ultraconformal deposition, Mofat et al.<sup>10</sup> observed bottom up filling of cobalt in 8 μm × 56 μm silicon through-holes. They achieved this by utilizing polyethylenimine (PEI) as an inhibitor. Jungkyu Kang et al.<sup>11,12</sup> found that void-free filling could be achieved even in low aspect ratio trenches in the presence of benzimidazole (BZI) and 2-mercaptobenzimida zole (MBI). An et al. demonstrated the potential application of nitrogen-containing organic heterocyclic molecules, nitro blue tetrazolium chloride (NBT)<sup>13</sup> and malachite green (MG),<sup>14</sup> as inhibitors. Their research found that the heterocyclic structures of the additive molecules preferentially adsorb on the cathode surface, serving as a mechanism to inhibit cobalt deposition. Huang et al.<sup>15−17</sup> utilized electrochemical methods such as EQCM and cyclic voltammetry to investigate the inhibitory properties of oxime-containing compounds, including cyclo hexanedione dioxime (CHD), furandione dioxime (FD), and dimethylglyoxime (DMG), on cobalt electrodeposition. However, the actual pore-filling performance and the micro scopic mechanisms involved still require further exploration He et al.<sup>18,19</sup> studied the inhibitory efects of polyvinylpyrro lidone (PVP) using cyclic voltammetry and other electro chemical methods, finding that PVP efectively inhibited cobalt electrodeposition, and that Cl<sup>−</sup> enhanced this inhibitory efect. In the field of cobalt interconnects, due to cobalt’s lower reduction potential compared to hydrogen’s evolution potential, hydrogen evolution reactions are inevitably occurring during the cobalt deposition process.<sup>20</sup> To mitigate this side reaction, researchers have employed additives with hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) inhibition capabilities,<sup>20</sup> including alkynyl/alkenyl additives. Pan et al.<sup>21</sup> suggested that brightener butynediol may adsorb on the Co metal surface and be reduced by adsorbed hydrogen produced by the side reaction. Kiruba et al.<sup>22</sup> extracted organic products from cobalt plating solutions containing butynediol and confirmed via Raman spectroscopy that butynediol was catalytically converted into butenediol on the cobalt surface. Wu et al.<sup>23</sup> investigated alkynol additives such as 1,4-butynediol (BYD), 1,4-butenediol (BED), and ethylene glycol (EG), which contains only −OH functional groups, to elucidate the potential mechanisms of unsaturated carbon bonds in cobalt electrodeposition. However, research on the application of alkynyl/alkenyl additives in bottom-up cobalt filling is scarce. This study selected 5-ethynylpyrimidine (5-EP), a compound containing unsaturated carbon bonds, as a novel inhibitor for cobalt electrodeposition. The study utilized electrochemical techni ques, namely cyclic voltammetry (CV) and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), to examine the inhibitory impact of the ethynyl group
( - \mathrm { C } \mathrm { \equiv } \mathrm { C } - )

on cobalt electrodeposition and to assess its efects on cobalt deposition. Chronoamperometry (I−T) tests and fitting were conducted to analyze the nucleation process of cobalt during the plating process. The experiment used a platinum electrode with a rotating disk (Pt-RDE) as the working electrode (WE), which had a diameter of 5 mm. paragraph_content.content: 3.1.2. Cathodic Polarization Curve. Linear scanning voltammetry (LSV) was used to evaluate the inhibitory efect of the inhibitor (5-EP) on the cobalt deposition process. The evaluation was carried out at two diferent rotational speeds: 2000 and 200 rpm. The relevant results are shown in Figure 2. With the addition of 5-EP, it can be noticed that the overpotential increases, and the additive adsorbs on the surface of the electrode, forming a film of material that causes the electrochemical reaction to take place on this film rather than on the electrode surface. In this case, the additives may occupy the active sites on the electrode surface, leading to a negative potential shift.<sup>24,25</sup> Regardless of the rotational speed setting, it is found that the addition of 5-EP leads to a steady shift of the reduction potential in a negative direction. This suggests that the inhibitor (5-EP) increases the cathodic polarization and prevents the reduction of

at the cathode. In addition, the ability of 5-EP to inhibit cobalt deposition was significantly higher at high speeds than at low speeds. This finding is consistent with the results of the CV analysis, suggesting that 5-EP has a significant ability to inhibit cobalt accumulation in the inner wall of the blind hole.

paragraph_content.content: 3.4. Blind Hole Filling Experiment. Based on the electrochemical experimental findings, it is anticipated that the inclusion of additives would enhance the electroplating and filling of cobalt in blind holes. Therefore, an experiment was conducted to examine the impact of the inhibitor molecule (5- EP) on blind hole filling with cobalt. Figure 7 illustrates the cross-sectional images of blind hole filled cobalt deposited at various time intervals. As depicted in Figure 7a, when 6 ppm of 5-EP was added to the electrolyte for electroplating, a Vshaped filling of cobalt deposition in the blind hole was observed after 3 h, due to convection and mass transfer efects. Figure 7b shows that with increased electroplating time, the cobalt layer in the blind hole exhibited a bottom-up filling trend, although superfilling was not yet achieved. As shown in Figure 7c, after 5 h of electroplating, the blind hole was completely filled without voids or gaps. This indicates that 5- EP initially adsorbs at the mouth of the blind hole during the electroplating process, inhibiting cobalt deposition at the entrance. Due to the relatively slow mass transfer rate of 5-EP from the solution to the micropores, the replenishment rate of 5-EP at the bottom is lower than its consumption rate, forming a concentration gradient, ultimately achieving bottom-up superfilling of the blind hole. The blind hole filling experiments further illuminates that the inhibitor (5-EP) is an excellent material for achieving cobalt superfilling.

3.5. Characterization. 3.5.1. SEM/AFM Characterization. The surface morphology of the cobalt deposited from the electrolyte with diferent concentrations of the inhibitor (5- EP) was analyzed using SEM. The relevant SEM data are displayed in Figure 9. Figure 9a clearly shows that the cobalt coating obtained from the electroplating solution with additives has a rough and porous surface, characterized by the presence of massive growth clusters. The presence of the inhibitor (5-EP) clearly alters the micro morphology of the cobalt coating. As shown in Figure 8b−d, introducing an inhibitor (5-EP) can efectively improve the quality of the cobalt layer. When 2 ppm of inhibitor (5-EP) was added, the cobalt particle size decreased. When the concentration of inhibitor (5-EP) was increased to 4 ppm, the cobalt particle size was further reduced, and the surface of the plated layer was smooth. When the inhibitor (5-EP) is added up to 6 ppm, the cobalt grain size on the coated surface is minimized, and the coating is smooth and flat in the macroscopic state. This suggests that the inhibitor (5-EP) has the ability to significantly enhance the surface structure of the cobalt coating, resulting in increased density.

The efect of diferent concentrations of the inhibitor (5-EP) on the cobalt deposit under constant current conditions was studied using AFM.<sup>34</sup> Figure 10 exhibits the results. Figure 10a,b demonstrate that the surface roughness, Sa, of the cobalt deposit in the basic electrolyte without the inhibitor (5-EP) measures 24.80 nm. Nevertheless, the presence of the inhibitor (5-EP) leads to a notable reduction in the surface roughness of the cobalt deposit. Figure 10c−g demonstrate that the addition of 6 ppm of 5-EP throughout the electroplating process results in a surface roughness of Sa = 2.15 nm for the cobalt deposit after completion. This suggests that the inhibitor (5-EP) has the ability to enhance the consistency of the cobalt layer throughout the process of cobalt electrodeposition.

paragraph_content.content: 3.5.4. Contact Angle Test. The wettability of the electrolyte to the electrode is an important parameter during electro deposition. Here the surface contact angle meter (Kruss K100- MK2) was used to measure the contact angle value of the plating solution containing a leveling agent on the surface of the plated layer after diferent plating times. The PCB boards with plating times of 1−5 h were prepared in advance and cleaned with deionized water, and
5 \mu \mathrm { L }

Figure 13 shows the contact angle (CA) value of the droplets on the PCB with diferent deposition times. As shown in Figure 13, the contact angle of the blank control sample is greater than 30°, and with the increase of deposition time, the contact angle gradually becomes smaller, respectively, 76.1, 52.8, 34.4, 20.7, and

. The small value of CA indicates that the interfacial energy between the electrolyte and the surface of the plated layer is higher, and the easier it is to be wetted. This result implies the inhibitor (5-EP) can significantly reduce the surface tension of the plating solution and improve its wettability. The reduction in the surface tension is also beneficial for removing the absorbed hydrogen during the cobalt plating process promptly and improving the quality of the plated layer.
